Field surveys of Silver grunt (Pomadasys argenteus) in the coastal waters of the Indo-Pacific have provided detailed morphometric data, revealing that the species attains an ultimate total length of 70 centimeters [Li = 70 centimeters]. This maximum size, recorded from long-term gillnet sampling, positions Pomadasys argenteus as one of the larger members of its genus within the region. In conjunction with this asymptotic dimension, the length at which individuals first achieve reproductive competence has been documented through gonad inspection across multiple size classes; the total length at puberty was determined to be 30.6 centimeters [Lp = 30.6 centimeters]. This threshold marks the onset of gonadal maturation and is a critical parameter for understanding the species' demographic structure, as it indicates that about half of the asymptotic body length must be attained before reproductive contribution begins, a pattern consistent with many iteroparous haemulids.

The early life stages of Silver grunt are characterized by a brief and energetically constrained developmental window. Newly emerged prolarvae, immediately following eclosion, possess an extremely small body size; the wet weight at birth has been estimated at 0.00027 grams [Wwb = 0.00027 grams], a value derived from the typical egg diameter of 0.8 millimeters and reflecting the limited endogenous yolk reserves available to the lecithotrophic larva. The duration of this yolk-dependent phase is tightly linked to ambient temperature, and under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C], the age at birth—defined as the moment of chorion rupture and larval emergence—was recorded as 4.5 days [ab = 4.5 days]. This rapid development is an adaptive response to high predation pressure on pelagic eggs and vulnerable prolarvae, ensuring that the transition to exotrophic feeding occurs before endogenous reserves are fully depleted.

Reproductive output in Pomadasys argenteus has been quantified from gravid females captured during the spawning season. At a body length of 58 centimeters, a single female was found to contain 286,520 ova, which translates to a daily reproduction rate of approximately 785 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 785 eggs per day] when spread across the typical annual spawning interval. The high fecundity is typical of batch-spawning teleosts and reflects a life-history strategy that compensates for high larval mortality through the production of numerous small, pelagic eggs. Such a reproductive pattern is common among haemulids inhabiting tropical shelf environments where food resources for larvae are seasonally abundant but spatially patchy.

As individuals progress through the juvenile and sub-adult stages, somatic growth continues until the ultimate body mass is approached. The ultimate wet weight of Pomadasys argenteus, derived from length-weight regressions based on extensive field sampling, reaches approximately 4,300 grams [Wwi = approximately 4,300 grams]. This asymptotic mass is attained after several years of steady growth and represents the maximum body size that the species can sustain given the energetic constraints of its demersal feeding ecology, which primarily targets benthic crustaceans and small mollusks. In comparison to other haemulids of similar maximum length, the ultimate wet weight observed in Silver grunt aligns closely with predictions from general teleost length-weight allometry, suggesting a consistent body shape and condition factor across populations in the region.

Longevity records for Silver grunt, based on otolith increment analysis from individuals collected in the northern Indian Ocean, indicate that the lifespan of this species reaches up to 12 years [am = up to 12 years] under natural conditions at a mean annual water temperature of 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C], consistent with the species' tropical distribution. The relatively extended lifespan compared to other small-bodied haemulids is likely linked to a moderate growth rate and delayed onset of senescence, allowing multiple reproductive seasons over the course of an individual's life. Such a long reproductive window, combined with high fecundity, suggests that even moderate fishing pressure on adult stocks could have delayed but significant impacts on population resilience, emphasizing the need for size-based management strategies.
